::: {#exm-beta-bernoulli}
#### Beta-Bernoulli updating

Let $\dsn{Y} \siid \Bernoulli(\prob)$ given $\prob$,
with $r = \sumin y_i$ successes,
and let the prior for $\prob$ be a $\operatorname{Beta}(a, b)$ distribution,
whose density is proportional to $\prob^{a-1}(1-\prob)^{b-1}$ on $(0, 1)$.
The likelihood is

$$
\ba
\p(\vy \mid \prob)
&= \prodin \prob^{y_i}(1-\prob)^{1-y_i}
&& \text{(independent Bernoulli observations)}\\
&= \prob^{\sum_i y_i}(1-\prob)^{n - \sum_i y_i}
&& \text{(adding exponents)}\\
&= \prob^{r}(1-\prob)^{n-r}
&& \text{(definition of $r$)}.
\ea
$$

By @cor-bayes-proportional,

$$
\ba
\p(\prob \mid \vy)
&\propto \prob^{r}(1-\prob)^{n-r} \cdot \prob^{a-1}(1-\prob)^{b-1}
&& \text{(likelihood times prior)}\\
&= \prob^{a + r - 1}(1-\prob)^{b + n - r - 1}
&& \text{(adding exponents)},
\ea
$$

which is proportional to the $\operatorname{Beta}(a + r,\; b + n - r)$ density.
So the Beta family is conjugate to the Bernoulli likelihood.
The prior parameters $a$ and $b$ act as *pseudo-counts*
of prior successes and failures:
the posterior adds the $r$ observed successes and $n - r$ observed failures to them.

The uniform prior of @exm-prior is $\operatorname{Beta}(1, 1)$.
With that prior and $r = 55$ successes in $n = 91$ trials,
the posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(56, 37)$,
with this mean and equal-tailed 95% [credible interval](#def-credible-interval):

```{r}
#| label: beta-bernoulli-posterior
#| code-fold: false
a_post <- 1 + 55
b_post <- 1 + 91 - 55
post_summary <- c(
  mean = a_post / (a_post + b_post),
  lower = stats::qbeta(0.025, a_post, b_post),
  upper = stats::qbeta(0.975, a_post, b_post)
) |>
  round(3)
post_summary
```

The mean uses the $\operatorname{Beta}(a, b)$ mean $a / (a + b)$
[@CaseBerg01, Section 3.3, p. 107].
By @def-credible-interval,
the interval is read as a probability statement about $\prob$ itself:
given these 91 trials,
the posterior probability that $\prob$ lies between
`r post_summary[["lower"]]` and `r post_summary[["upper"]]` is 0.95
(approximately, since those endpoints are rounded to three decimals).
A 95% confidence interval computed from the same data
supports no such statement,
as @sec-bayes-interval-interp explains:
its 0.95 describes the procedure over repeated samples,
and the realized interval either contains $\prob$ or does not.
:::
